> @arbrauns Do you have any technical reason for using the ST HAL MMC stack instead of the Zephyr MMC stack?

What exactly is the "Zephyr MMC stack"? `subsys/sd/mmc.c`? That seems to use the `sdhc` driver class, which as far as I can tell is not implemented for the STM32 SDMMC peripheral.

> That seems to use the `sdhc` driver class, which as far as I can tell is not implemented for the STM32 SDMMC peripheral.

Indeed, it's not implemented.

> > @arbrauns Do you have any technical reason for using the ST HAL MMC stack instead of the Zephyr MMC stack?
> 
> What exactly is the "Zephyr MMC stack"? `subsys/sd/mmc.c`? That seems to use the `sdhc` driver class, which as far as I can tell is not implemented for the STM32 SDMMC peripheral.

Yes, I mean the MMC implementation in the SD subsystem. I was asking if there is any reason other than the SDHC driver not being implemented yet.

> Yes, I mean the MMC implementation in the SD subsystem. I was asking if there is any reason other than the SDHC driver not being implemented yet.

No, if there was an SDHC driver, that'd be preferable, since it probably makes it easier to support both SD cards and eMMC with the same firmware - even if not "properly", at least I'd only have to hack zephyr, not both zephyr and the ST HAL.

> Yes, I mean the MMC implementation in the SD subsystem. I was asking if there is any reason other than the SDHC driver not being implemented yet.

Reason is that current STM32 HAL is not providing this exact API level. There is an on going effort to fix this and it should be available later this year. Current implementation of the driver was gran fathered since available way before the SD subsystem was made available.
In the mean time, I propose not to block current contribution and wait the new HAL API to be available before migrating the driver to the "new" SD subsystem.

Perhaps I'm confused, but this doesn't quite make sense to me. Wouldn't an SDMMC compatible driver using the LL functions be most appropriate for integrating with the Zephyr kernel?

> Perhaps I'm confused, but this doesn't quite make sense to me. Wouldn't an SDMMC compatible driver using the LL functions be most appropriate for integrating with the Zephyr kernel?

Would you mind clarifying what doesn't make sense ?

Usually when I've read peripheral drivers in Zephyr they're written directly to the peripheral, instead of through an abstracted driver from the SoC manufacturer. It seems like the plan is to wrap the U5 HAL_SDIOx layer, introducing dependencies on HAL_RCC, and so forth instead of keeping all of the driver native to Zephyr.

> Usually when I've read peripheral drivers in Zephyr they're written directly to the peripheral

On the contrary, using vendor HAL is rather common. 95% of STM32 peripheral drivers use either LL or HAL, and STM32 is not an exception on this topic.

Sure, this isn't uncommon. Drivers are ofen using some amount of vendor HAL/LL drivers. Most often, for STM32 platforms, I see use of LL to simplify the register access etc. as a small step above using the SoC specific header, and all of the state is in a bespoke Zephyr structure/context. Use of the STM32 HAL stuff isn't as common. (My cross section here is ADC, CAN, flash, serial/uart, I2C, I2S, GPIO, DMA, clock. _**All**_ of them use LL and eschew the HAL drviers.) Frankly, this makes a ton more sense to me than using the HAL drivers provided by ST. These drivers are all tight and integrate well with their Zephyr driver APIs as a result. Using the HAL drivers (almost) always comes with a dependency on HAL_RCCx and HAL_DMAx - which again are handled elsewhere by the Zephyr drivers.

It just seems to me that the HAL driver is often too much to bring along for Zephyr with it's strong device driver model and existing non-HAL drivers. A large appeal of Zephyr is that it provides not only the kernel _but also_ the HAL/drivers. All of the most core drivers are written around LL, and I think for good reason. It's disappointing to see new drivers just wrapping specific HAL drivers and bringing along their dependencies - even though I do understand the additional effort to write a Zephyr specific driver from scratch isn't always justified. I just don't want to see a HAL driver for RCC, DMA, and GPIO along side of the Zephyr ones just because I wanted to mount an SD card.

And, hey, look - having a driver that wraps HAL may not be as nice as a driver in tree but it's better than nothing. Just because I'd prefer having it in tree obviously isn't a blocker. I'm just advocating for what I'd like to see.

>  I just don't want to see a HAL driver for RCC, DMA, and GPIO along side of the Zephyr ones just because I wanted to mount an SD card.

This is not quite the real picture. They're are quite few dependencies, so I general, you'll only see a couple of those functions used, not a whole driver per se. The only real functional overcross with is the DMA, which is unfortunate but didn't lead to any issue so far from what I know.

Also note that the choice of HAL is not considered lightly. In most cases they are used because:
- They are chosen on complex IPs where making use of mature high level functionalities provided by HAL greatly fasten the development and simplify maintenance
- When the IP is used, it is general used with a stack and a large application, making the footprint diff between LL and HAL negligible in the overall binary size
- There are no LL equivalent (which is the case for eth, USB, and .. SDIO today)

Finally, if someone would stand up to develop and maintain an LL equivalent driver, we'll consider it for sure. But, to the notable exception of CAN, I haven't see any developer volunteering for such task, unfortunately.

> This is not quite the real picture. They're are quite few dependencies, so I general, you'll only see a couple of those functions used, not a whole driver per se. The only real functional overcross with is the DMA, which is unfortunate but didn't lead to any issue so far from what I know.

That's a good point - the unused parts of the dependencies should get stripped. I had a project in the past jump up ~8 kB when adding a HAL driver because of the RCC/DMA/etc. dependencies alone. In large projects that probably makes less of an impact but in that case it was too much to bear and I had to write a driver from scratch so things fit. Maybe that's just personal "baggage" I'm carrying.

> * There are no LL equivalent (which is the case for eth, USB, and .. SDIO today)

This is where I disagree. There _is_ an SDMMC LL driver for the SDMMC peripheral that functions as the basis for this driver. In fact, both the HAL SD and SDIO drivers leverage the LL driver extensively. In my mind, an in-tree driver would leverage the SDMMC LL driver in the same way, just as the UART/I2C/etc. drivers currently do.

> Finally, if someone would stand up to develop and maintain an LL equivalent driver, we'll consider it for sure.

Frankly, I'd like to be able to do this, but the product at my day job that would justify this keeps getting postponed. 😠 Not the fault of anyone in this discussion. I just haven't been free to volunteer to do this yet. That may change in the future. In the interest of that, is there a good development board with eMMC/SD that would be suitable for driver testing/validation? What is ST planning on using/uses for validation of Cube drivers?

> But, to the notable exception of CAN, I haven't see any developer volunteering for such task, unfortunately.

Well, not everyone can be @henrikbrixandersen 😉 I don't know how he does it.

> This is where I disagree. There is an SDMMC LL driver for the SDMMC peripheral that functions as the basis for this driver.

Well, the SDMMC LL header is not actually a public API as per STM32Cube programming policy, it's only there for private HAL usage. I agree the naming is confusing. It's only a set of utility functions and not a complete set of functions designed to allow implementation of complete driver. I don't say it can't be done, just that's it's not meant to be used that way, and I'd prefer avoiding to open the door to exotic implementations that could lead to unexpected maintenance issues (for instance, as it's not supposed to be used solely, the file could disappear in future Cube evolution).
That's an interesting twist. Good to know it's not really meant to be a public API - I've been using it as one for a while now on a project to cover places the HAL drivers didn't.

issue_context.title: sdmmc_stm32 disk driver will not work with eMMC
issue_context.body:
**Is your enhancement proposal related to a problem? Please describe.**
There are two distinct protocols used over the SDMMC bus: 
* JEDEC JESD84-B51A: Embedded MultiMediaCard (e.MMC), Electrical Standard (5.1A).
* SD Card "SD Specifications"
While these two standards have much in common, they also have crucial differences in the protocol (especially during device initialization). 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The attached patch adds a new disk driver for the STM32 family of SOCs to utilize the MMC protocol instead of the SD. The 2 drivers are very similar (indeed, I converted the SDCard driver to the emmc driver with simple global edits), and it might be possible to combine them better. However, this is a simple and effective solution that will allow developers to target either type of device.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
My initial approach was to edit the `sdmmc_stm32.c` disk driver In place. However, I understand that this could break existing users that do rely on the SD protocol.

[patch.tar.gz](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/files/6672237/patch.tar.gz)
